html:
A confederation of Turkic nomads on the steppes of what is now eastern and northern Kazakhstan, strongest in the 10th century. The Kimeks led it from the Irtysh river; the Kipchaks were its western wing. The map shows it in 1000.

It grew out of the turmoil after the Uyghur Khaganate fell in 840, part of the long westward drift of Turkic peoples. Muslim geographers describe the Kimeks as herders who also fished, hunted for fur and kept some winter towns. To the south lay the Oghuz and the Muslim lands of the Samanids.

In the 11th century the Kimek centre weakened and the Kipchaks took the lead. They moved west across the steppe and, joined with the Cumans, became the Cuman-Kipchak confederation that later faced Kievan Rus' and the Mongols.
